passage: In the changing room at his Dublin school, Daniel's voice cracked mid-sentence. Yuki burst out laughing. Daniel went red and wanted to disappear. That evening he asked his dad, quietly, "Is something wrong with my voice? And I've got spots now." His dad sat down with him. "Nothing's wrong. Your body's starting to change. Your voice will settle. Showering every day and using deodorant helps with the sweaty part." Daniel nodded, relieved. The next day, when Yuki's own voice squeaked in class, Daniel just smiled and didn't laugh.

qa.a: It cracked mid-sentence.

qa.q: What does Daniel going red and wanting to disappear show about how he felt?
qa.a: It shows he felt embarrassed and ashamed of the change in his voice.

qa.q: What helped Daniel feel less ashamed?
qa.a: His dad explained calmly that his body was changing normally and gave simple hygiene tips.

qa.q: How might Yuki feel when Daniel doesn't laugh at Yuki's squeak?

grounding: It shows a boy understanding early puberty and hygiene without shame.

A week later, a pad fell out of a girl's bag in the corridor. Sachin began to snigger. Anirban said, "Leave it, it's normal. We learned it," and kept walking. The girl picked it up without looking embarrassed.

passage: I'm Kiran, Sudha's older sister. Sudha is eleven, and last month she got her first period at school. She came home quiet and went straight to her room. I knocked. I told her it happened to me too, and Mummy sat with us and explained it properly. Now Sudha keeps a small pouch in her bag with pads and a spare pair of shorts, and she even told her friend what to do if it happens to her.

passage: Seema, you asked why I always say 'ask me anything'. Let me tell you. When I was twelve, in our village, nobody explained anything to girls. One morning I saw blood and thought I was dying. I hid in the cowshed and cried. My mother just said, 'Keep quiet, don't tell anyone,' and gave me old cloth. I felt dirty for months, as if I'd done something wrong. Only when my aunt came visiting did she sit me down, say 'Leela, listen,' and tell me it was my body growing up, that it happens to every girl. I promised myself my girls would know before. So, Seema, your voice-changing brother, your own body, all of it: ask me anything.

qa.q: Where did young Leela hide when she first saw the blood?
qa.a: She hid in the cowshed and cried.

qa.q: Why did young Leela feel dirty for months?
qa.a: She felt ashamed and frightened, because nobody explained what was happening and she was told to keep quiet, so she believed she had done something wrong.

qa.q: What is Leela doing differently for Seema?
qa.a: She is inviting open questions about body changes early, so Seema can learn facts before any fear or shame sets in.

qa.q: How might Seema feel hearing Leela's story?
qa.a: Seema might feel sad for young Leela and more comfortable bringing questions to Leela.

grounding: An elder recalls puberty without information and now offers a young listener shame-free understanding.

It was sports day, the sun was hot, and Lalremsiami, twelve, was about to run the relay when she felt something wet. She went pale. Her first period, and she had nothing with her.
Her friend Charu saw her face. “What's wrong?”
Lalremsiami whispered.
Charu didn't laugh. She took off her jacket and tied it round Lalremsiami's waist. “Come. Mrs Lalhmangaihi has pads in the sick room.”
The teacher gave her a pad and a clean pair of shorts, showed her the washroom and said, “This is normal. Nothing to be ashamed of. Next time, keep a spare in your bag.”
Lalremsiami ran the last leg of the relay after all.

qa.q: How did Lalremsiami feel when she realised her period had started?

passage:
At the school in Chennai, Ms Rehana, the counsellor, ran a Friday talk for Class 6 girls. A box on her desk was for questions without names.
Gopika, eleven, wrote hers during the break: Why do I smell sweaty now even when I'm not running? Is something wrong with me?
Ms Rehana read it out, without saying whose. “Good question. Nothing is wrong. As bodies grow, sweat changes. Bathing daily, clean clothes, and washing under the arms help. It happens to everyone, boys too.”
Some girls giggled, then nodded.
Gopika didn't feel embarrassed any more. She felt normal.

qa.q: What was the box on Ms Rehana's desk for?
qa.a: Questions without names.

qa.q: How did Gopika feel after Ms Rehana answered her question?
qa.a: She felt relieved and normal instead of embarrassed.

qa.q: Why was the question box a good idea?
qa.a: It let students ask about body changes privately, without shame.

qa.q: How might the other girls feel after hearing the answer?
qa.a: They may feel relieved too, since many probably had the same question.

grounding: An eleven-year-old learns about body changes and hygiene without shame through an anonymous question box.

“Leela-didi, can I play football during my period? Sonam said you shouldn't run or it's dangerous.”
Leela put down her book. “That's not true, Mahima. Lots of girls play sports on their period.”
“Really?”
“If you feel okay, you can play. Some days you might feel tired or have cramps. Then you can rest.”
“What if it leaks?”
“Keep a spare pad and shorts in your bag. And tell your coach if you need a break. It's normal.”
Mahima thought. “And if it really hurts a lot?”
“Tell Mumma. If it keeps going or worries you, we'll check with the doctor.”
Mahima picked up her football boots. “Okay. Practice at four.”

qa.a: Sonam said you shouldn't run or it's dangerous.

qa.q: How did Mahima feel about playing football during her period?
qa.a: She felt worried and unsure because of what Sonam said.

qa.q: What practical tips did Leela give?
qa.a: Keep a spare pad and shorts, rest if tired, tell the coach if needed, and tell Mumma if pain keeps going.

qa.q: How does Leela see Sonam's claim?
qa.a: Leela sees it as a myth and calmly corrects it.

grounding: An older sister corrects a period myth and helps an eleven-year-old without shame.

passage:
I'm Zeenat. I still remember the day in Class 6 when I got my first period at school. I saw a stain on my skirt in the washroom and my hands went cold. I thought everyone would laugh.
I went to our class teacher. She didn't make a face. She took me to the sick room, gave me a pad and a spare skirt, and showed me how to use it. She said, "This is normal. It happens to girls as they grow."
When I got home, my little brother Tarun asked why Ammi was giving me a hot water bag. Ammi just told him the truth, simply. He said "Oh," and went back to his cartoons.
That was it. No big deal.

Madhav came to see me today. He said his voice keeps cracking in class and two boys call him "squeaky". He'd also noticed hair growing under his arms and asked if something was wrong with him.

Dear Diary,
Today something happened. I got my period. I was at home, thank god. Amma is in Chennai for Paati's operation, so it was just Appa.
I didn't know how to tell him. I stood outside his room for ages. Finally I said, "Appa, I think I got my period."
He didn't look embarrassed. He said, "Okay. Good that you told me." He went to the medical shop and came back with pads. He'd even asked the shop lady which kind.
Then he made me hot milk and said, "If it hurts, tell me." Amma called and asked if I was okay. I said yes. I meant it.
— Kavitha

On the third day of the paddy harvest, Devika woke to a dark stain on her mat and froze. Her mother was already in the field. She wrapped her shawl around her waist and ran to the back of the house where her cousin Gurpreet was drawing water.
"Didi, I think I'm hurt."
Gurpreet looked, then smiled gently. "You're not hurt. This is your period. It happened to me at eleven too."
She took Devika inside, closed the door and showed her a clean pad from her own tin, how to put it on, and how to wrap the used one in paper before throwing it away. "Bathe as usual," she said. "Anyone who says a bath makes it worse is wrong."
Devika still felt shy. But when she walked out to the field, she held her head up.

qa.q: What did Gurpreet show Devika inside the house?
qa.a: Gurpreet showed her a clean pad from her own tin, how to put it on, and how to wrap the used one in paper before throwing it away.

qa.q: What did Devika feel when she first saw the stain, and what shows it?
qa.a: Devika felt scared and confused, which shows when she froze and told Gurpreet she thought she was hurt.

qa.q: What small step helped Devika feel less ashamed?
qa.a: Gurpreet closed the door for privacy and calmly said it had happened to her too, which made it normal instead of embarrassing.

qa.q: What would change if Devika had had nobody to ask that morning?
qa.a: She might have stayed frightened, believed wrong ideas about baths, or hidden it; having someone calm made her period something she could manage.

grounding: Shows a girl's first period handled with privacy, simple hygiene steps and no shame, correcting a common myth.

Christmas in Brisbane is sweaty, and carol practice was in a hall with one fan. Rafael was halfway through a solo line when his voice cracked, high then low. A couple of the younger kids giggled.
Rafael went red and stopped. Wei, his friend from the tenor row, leaned over. "Mine did that all last term. It's just your voice getting deeper."
After practice the choir teacher took Rafael aside, not in front of the others. She said a changing voice was normal at his age and he could sing the lower part until it settled.
On the walk home, Wei also muttered, "And, uh, bring deodorant after PE. Nobody told me. Mum did, eventually." Rafael laughed. He added it to his list.

I'm Kishore, Arnab's cousin, and I'm sixteen. At the Durga Puja recitation this year, Arnab, twelve, stood up to read, and his voice cracked in the middle of a line, high then low. Some younger kids giggled. Arnab went red and sat down fast.
After, I found him behind the pandal. He muttered, "Something's wrong with my voice. And I smell weird after football."
I told him mine did the same at his age and that it's just the body growing up. His father came over, heard us, and said gently, "Nothing is wrong. Voices change, sweat changes. A daily bath, clean clothes and a deodorant help. Ask me anything, anytime."
I don't know what Arnab was thinking, but the next evening he read again. His voice cracked once. He kept going.

qa.a: His voice cracked in the middle of a line, high then low.

qa.q: What was Arnab probably feeling when he sat down fast?
qa.a: He was probably embarrassed and worried, thinking something was wrong with his body.

qa.q: How did Arnab's father help without making him feel ashamed?
qa.a: He said calmly that the changes were normal, gave simple hygiene tips, and invited Arnab to ask him anything, anytime.

qa.a: Because Kishore went through the same changes, he can reassure his cousin that it's normal and make him feel less alone.

grounding: Shows a child learning about puberty changes and hygiene calmly, without shame or myths.
